newsitem.title: USA: Ford pact sets job precedents, may hurt GM.
newsitem.headline: Ford pact sets job precedents, may hurt GM.

text.p: Ford Motor Co.'s tentative labour agreement with the United Auto Workers offers generous economic gains and sets new precedents for preserving jobs that are likely to cause problems for General Motors Corp., analysts said Tuesday.

Based on details that have trickled out since the deal was struck Monday night, the three-year deal looks like a major victory for the union, analysts said, due to Ford's committment to maintain employment for 95 percent of its 105,000-member hourly UAW work force.

The deal for the first time puts limits on a Big Three automaker's ability to shrink its work force. According to union and industry sources, Ford must maintain a specified hourly employment level at each of its 49 U.S. parts and assembly plants and at other facilites.
The pact will require Ford to replace thousands of employees due to retire over the next several years and maintain nearly 100,000 UAW hourly jobs.
"On the surface, it's a little more generous than I'd like to see, not only for Ford but for Chrysler and especially GM," said J.P. Morgan auto analyst David Bradley.

On economics, the deal gives workers a $2,000 bonus in the first year, and base-wage increases of 3 percent in the final two years, an improvement over the current pact, which offered a base wage gain in only one year and lump-sum payments in subsequent years.

The deal also includes significantly improved pension benefits, a key demand by many Ford workers expected to retire soon. The monthly payment rises to up to $2,260 a month from an average of $2,030 currently.

Both Ford and the union have declined to confirm any details of the agreement, which the union's executive board was scheduled to consider in a meeting Tuesday. The UAW's Ford Council, made up of plant-level leaders, is expected to vote on the pact Wednesday.
UAW President Stephen Yokich said Monday that Ford's rank-and-file workers are expected to vote on the pact next Monday, Sept. 23.
Analysts said they expected the pact to contain some kind of innovative benefit that would allow Ford to maintain its competitiveness.
"I suspect that there are side agreements and special terms to the new contracts that mitigate some of the negative impact," Bradley said.

Sources said the automaker will benefit from a new lower wage at parts plants for new work that Ford takes back from outside suppliers. The automaker also got to keep its three-year "grow-in" period for new hires, in which they start at 70 percent of full wages and reach parity with veteran workers after three years.
Analysts said Chrysler Corp. can likely afford to meet the terms of the Ford pact if it is imposed as a pattern agreement, but said GM will have a difficult time with it.

The world's largest automaker needs to shed 50,000 to 60,000 jobs over the next several years to reach Ford's level of productivity, and the contract will severely restrict GM's ability to shrink its workforce, said Lehman Brothers auto analyst Joseph Phillippi.
"It certainly doesn't look like something GM could ever sign," Phillippi said. "They've got to be going nuts over this."
GM's resistance could lead to a strike, which could be just as costly for the automaker, analysts said.
But Yokich has said he does not want a pattern agreement that leaves any one of the Big Three automakers at a major disadvantage. Analysts said he may be willing to cut a more lenient deal for GM.

"I think the UAW is willing to give GM a deal that is less onerous than the Ford deal is on its face, but certainly not what they want," said Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. analyst Ronald Glantz. "When it is all said and done, GM will have to maintain higher insourcing than it wants to."
